description: Associations are the Wolfram Language's hash tables: ordered key-value maps written <|k -> v, ...|> with O(1) lookup and full support for the list operations. This category covers association construction and querying, the grouping and tallying functions used to summarize data, the Dataset/Query layer for structured tabular data, and the sparse array and Missing data structures.

tools.name: Association
tools.description: An ordered mapping from keys to values, written <|k1 -> v1, k2 -> v2|>. Keys may be any expression, lookup is constant time, and insertion order is preserved. Associations behave like lists for Map, Select, Sort and Part, but operate on values while keeping keys attached, which makes them the natural record and dictionary type.
tools.usage:
<|key1 -> val1, key2 -> val2, ...|>
Association[key1 -> val1, ...]
assoc[key]
assoc[[key]]
tools.example:
a = <|"x" -> 1, "y" -> 2|>;
a["x"]
Map[#^2 &, a]
Append[a, "z" -> 3]
Association[Thread[{"a", "b"} -> {1, 2}]]
tools.notes: assoc[key] and assoc[[key]] both look up a value but differ on missing keys: the first gives Missing["KeyAbsent", key], the second raises an error. Duplicate keys keep the last value.

tools.name: AssociationQ
tools.description: Tests whether an expression is a valid Association, returning True or False. Use it in argument patterns (a_?AssociationQ) to write functions that accept records, and to distinguish an Association from a list of rules. It returns False for a plain list of Rule objects even though they look similar.
tools.example:
AssociationQ[<|"a" -> 1|>]
AssociationQ[{"a" -> 1}]
f[r_?AssociationQ] := Keys[r];
f[<|1 -> "x"|>]

tools.name: Keys
tools.description: Gives the list of keys of an Association in their stored order, or the left-hand sides of a list of rules. An optional function argument is applied to each key as it is extracted. Keys works on nested associations level by level and on Dataset objects.
tools.example:
Keys[<|"a" -> 1, "b" -> 2|>]
Keys[{x -> 1, y -> 2}]
Keys[<|1 -> "a", 2 -> "b"|>, ToString]
Length[Keys[data]]

tools.name: Values
tools.description: Gives the list of values of an Association, or the right-hand sides of a list of rules, in stored order. Combined with Keys it converts an Association into two parallel lists. An optional function is applied to each value.
tools.example:
Values[<|"a" -> 1, "b" -> 2|>]
Total[Values[<|"a" -> 1, "b" -> 2|>]]
Values[{x -> 1, y -> 2}]
Values[data, N]
tools.notes: Most list functions already operate on the values of an Association directly, so Total[assoc] and Mean[assoc] work without calling Values.

tools.name: KeyValueMap
tools.description: Applies a two-argument function to each key and its value, returning a plain list of results. This is the standard way to produce formatted output or new structures from an Association when you need both parts. The order follows the Association's key order.
tools.notes: Use AssociationMap to go the other way (build an Association from keys) and Map to transform values while keeping the Association structure.

tools.name: KeyMap
tools.description: Applies a function to every key of an Association while leaving the values untouched, returning a new Association. Use it to normalize key names, convert strings to symbols, or strip prefixes. If the mapping makes two keys collide, the later value wins.
tools.example:
KeyMap[ToUpperCase, <|"a" -> 1, "b" -> 2|>]
KeyMap[ToString, <|1 -> "x", 2 -> "y"|>]
KeyMap[StringTrim, <|" a " -> 1|>]

tools.name: Lookup
tools.description: Looks up a key in an Association or list of rules, returning a default when the key is absent instead of a Missing object. Lookup[assoc, {k1, k2}] looks up several keys at once, and the operator form Lookup[key] composes in pipelines. It is the safe accessor for optional record fields.
tools.usage:
Lookup[assoc, key]
Lookup[assoc, key, default]
Lookup[assoc, {k1, k2, ...}]
Lookup[key][assoc]
tools.notes: The default argument is only evaluated if the key is missing, so an expensive fallback costs nothing in the common case.

tools.name: Key
tools.description: Wraps a key so it can be used inside Part when the key itself would otherwise be interpreted as a position. assoc[[Key[k]]] extracts the value for key k even when k is an integer or a list. It also appears in the positions returned by Position for Associations.
tools.notes: For string keys assoc[["k"]] works directly; Key is only required for integer keys, lists and other expressions that Part would read as positions.

tools.name: KeyExistsQ
tools.description: Tests whether an Association or list of rules contains a given key, returning True or False without extracting the value. It is the constant-time membership test that replaces MemberQ for dictionary-style data. The operator form KeyExistsQ[key] is convenient in Select.
tools.example:
KeyExistsQ[<|"a" -> 1|>, "a"]
KeyExistsQ[<|"a" -> 1|>, "b"]
Select[records, KeyExistsQ["email"]]
If[KeyExistsQ[opts, "verbose"], Print["on"]]

tools.name: KeyDrop
tools.description: Returns an Association with the given keys removed; keys that are not present are silently ignored. A list of keys drops several at once. Use it to strip internal or sensitive fields before exporting a record.
tools.example:
KeyDrop[<|"a" -> 1, "b" -> 2|>, "a"]
KeyDrop[<|"a" -> 1, "b" -> 2, "c" -> 3|>, {"a", "c"}]
KeyDrop["password"] /@ users

tools.name: KeyTake
tools.description: Returns an Association containing only the specified keys, in the order they are requested. Keys that do not exist are simply omitted from the result. It is the projection operation for records, the counterpart of KeyDrop.
tools.example:
KeyTake[<|"a" -> 1, "b" -> 2, "c" -> 3|>, {"a", "c"}]
KeyTake[{"name", "id"}] /@ records
KeyTake[config, "port"]

tools.name: KeySelect
tools.description: Keeps the elements of an Association whose keys satisfy a predicate, preserving both keys and values. Use it to filter columns by name, for example selecting every key that starts with a prefix. Select, by contrast, filters on values.
tools.example:
KeySelect[<|"ax" -> 1, "by" -> 2|>, StringStartsQ["a"]]
KeySelect[<|1 -> "a", 2 -> "b"|>, EvenQ]
KeySelect[data, StringContainsQ["temp"]]
tools.notes: KeyValueMap or Select[assoc, f] covers the value side; to filter on both, use Select on KeyValueMap output or Query.

tools.name: KeySort
tools.description: Reorders an Association so that its keys are in canonical (or custom) sorted order. An optional ordering function compares keys pairwise. Sorting keys makes two associations with the same content compare equal and produces predictable output order.
tools.example:
KeySort[<|"b" -> 2, "a" -> 1|>]
KeySort[<|3 -> c, 1 -> a, 2 -> b|>]
KeySort[<|"a" -> 1, "b" -> 2|>, Greater]

tools.name: KeySortBy
tools.description: Sorts an Association by the value of a function applied to each key, rather than by the keys themselves. Useful for ordering by a parsed date, a numeric suffix or a computed priority stored in the key. A list of functions gives tie-breaking keys.
tools.example:
KeySortBy[<|"item10" -> a, "item2" -> b|>, StringLength]
KeySortBy[<|"2024-03" -> 1, "2024-01" -> 2|>, DateObject]
KeySortBy[assoc, -# &]

tools.name: Merge
tools.description: Combines several Associations into one, applying a function to the list of values that share each key. Merge[{a1, a2}, Total] sums colliding values, Merge[..., Identity] keeps them all in a list, and Merge[..., Last] gives last-wins semantics. It is the general tool for aggregating records keyed the same way.
tools.example:
Merge[{<|"a" -> 1|>, <|"a" -> 2, "b" -> 3|>}, Total]
Merge[{<|"a" -> 1|>, <|"a" -> 2|>}, Identity]
Merge[{<|"x" -> 1|>, <|"x" -> 5|>}, Mean]
Merge[list_of_records, Flatten @* List]
tools.notes: The function always receives a list, even when only one association supplied a value for that key. Join[a1, a2] is simpler when you just want later values to win.

tools.name: AssociationMap
tools.description: Builds an Association by applying a function to each element of a list: AssociationMap[f, {a, b}] gives <|a -> f[a], b -> f[b]|>. With the option-free two-argument form the list supplies the keys and f computes the values. Giving f a two-element output form instead lets it produce key/value pairs directly.
tools.example:
AssociationMap[f, {a, b, c}]
AssociationMap[#^2 &, Range[5]]
AssociationMap[FileByteCount, FileNames["*.txt"]]
AssociationMap[PrimeQ, Range[10]]
tools.notes: AssociationThread is the choice when you already have separate key and value lists.

tools.name: AssociationThread
tools.description: Creates an Association from parallel lists of keys and values, the dictionary analogue of Thread. AssociationThread[keys -> values] and AssociationThread[keys, values] are both accepted. It is the fastest way to turn two columns into a lookup table.
tools.example:
AssociationThread[{"a", "b"} -> {1, 2}]
AssociationThread[Range[3], {x, y, z}]
AssociationThread[headers, row]
tools.notes: The two lists must be the same length. Duplicate keys collapse, keeping the last value.

tools.name: GroupBy
tools.description: Groups the elements of a list or Association into an Association keyed by the value of a function, optionally reducing each group with a second function. GroupBy[data, f] gives <|key -> {elements}|>, and GroupBy[data, f -> g, h] extracts g from each element and reduces the group with h. It is the split-apply-combine primitive for Wolfram Language data work.
tools.usage:
GroupBy[list, f]
GroupBy[list, f -> g]
GroupBy[list, f, h]
GroupBy[list, {f1, f2}]
tools.example:
GroupBy[Range[10], EvenQ]
GroupBy[{{"a", 1}, {"b", 2}, {"a", 3}}, First -> Last]
GroupBy[Range[10], EvenQ, Total]
GroupBy[records, #dept &, Mean[#salary & /@ #] &]
tools.notes: A list of grouping functions produces nested groups. Counts[f /@ list] is the shortcut when you only need group sizes.

tools.name: Counts
tools.description: Gives an Association mapping each distinct element of a list to the number of times it occurs. It is the one-pass histogram of categorical data and the fastest way to find the most common value. The result is ordered by first appearance; apply ReverseSort to rank by frequency.
tools.example:
Counts[{a, b, a, c, a}]
Counts[Characters["mississippi"]]
ReverseSort[Counts[words]]
First[Keys[ReverseSort[Counts[data]]]]
tools.notes: Tally returns the same information as a list of {value, count} pairs; Counts is usually more convenient because lookups are then O(1).

tools.name: CountsBy
tools.description: Counts elements according to the value of a function applied to each one, giving an Association from computed key to count. It combines Map and Counts in a single pass, so CountsBy[words, StringLength] tallies words by length. Equivalent to GroupBy[list, f, Length] but more direct.
tools.example:
CountsBy[Range[10], EvenQ]
CountsBy[{"apple", "fig", "kiwi"}, StringLength]
CountsBy[records, #category &]

tools.name: Tally
tools.description: Gives a list of {element, count} pairs for the distinct elements of a list, in order of first appearance. An optional two-argument test function treats near-equal elements as the same, which is useful for floating point data. Tally is the list-shaped alternative to Counts.
tools.example:
Tally[{a, b, a, c, b, a}]
Tally[RandomInteger[3, 20]]
Tally[{1.0, 1.001, 2.0}, Abs[#1 - #2] < 0.01 &]
SortBy[Tally[data], -Last[#] &]

tools.name: Gather
tools.description: Collects identical elements of a list into sublists, preserving the order of first appearance. An optional test function defines what counts as equivalent, allowing clustering by tolerance or by a custom relation. Gather is the unreduced form of Tally.
tools.notes: With an explicit test Gather is O(n^2); GatherBy with a key function is near-linear and usually preferable.

tools.name: GatherBy
tools.description: Groups list elements into sublists by the value of a function applied to each element, returning a list of groups rather than an Association. GatherBy[list, {f1, f2}] produces nested groupings. It is GroupBy without the keys, and is the right choice when only the partition matters.
tools.example:
GatherBy[Range[10], EvenQ]
GatherBy[{{1, a}, {2, b}, {1, c}}, First]
GatherBy[words, StringLength]
GatherBy[points, {First, Last}]

tools.name: Split
tools.description: Splits a list into runs of adjacent identical elements, keeping the original order. An optional test function splits wherever the test on two neighbouring elements fails, which makes it ideal for run-length encoding and for segmenting sorted or time-ordered data. Unlike Gather it only groups elements that are next to each other.
tools.example:
Split[{1, 1, 2, 3, 3, 3}]
Split[{1, 2, 4, 5, 7}, #2 == #1 + 1 &]
{First[#], Length[#]} & /@ Split[Characters["aaabbc"]]
tools.notes: Split on a sorted list is equivalent to Gather but much faster; sort first when grouping large datasets by value.

tools.name: SplitBy
tools.description: Splits a list into runs of adjacent elements that give the same value under a function. A list of functions splits hierarchically, producing nested runs. It is the segmentation tool for time series and log records that are already in order.
tools.example:
SplitBy[{1, 3, 5, 2, 4, 7}, EvenQ]
SplitBy[{{1, a}, {1, b}, {2, c}}, First]
SplitBy[events, DateValue[#date, "Day"] &]

tools.name: PositionIndex
tools.description: Gives an Association mapping each distinct value in a list to the list of positions where it occurs. It is the inverted index of a list and turns repeated Position searches into constant-time lookups. An optional function computes the key from each element.
tools.example:
PositionIndex[{a, b, a, c, a}]
PositionIndex[Characters["banana"]]
PositionIndex[Range[10], EvenQ]
PositionIndex[words]["the"]
tools.notes: Length /@ PositionIndex[list] gives the same result as Counts[list].

tools.name: Dataset
tools.description: A structured container for hierarchical and tabular data, built from nested lists and associations, that displays as an interactive table and supports query operations directly. Applying operators to a Dataset descends level by level, so ds[Select[...], "col"] filters rows then picks a column. It is the high-level interface for data analysis work in Mathematica.
tools.example:
ds = Dataset[{<|"name" -> "a", "v" -> 1|>, <|"name" -> "b", "v" -> 5|>}];
ds[All, "v"]
ds[Select[#v > 2 &]]
ds[Total, "v"]
ds[GroupBy["name"], Length]
tools.notes: Use Normal to convert a Dataset back into plain lists and associations, and SemanticImport or Import[..., "Dataset"] to build one from a file.

tools.name: Query
tools.description: Builds a composable query operator that descends through levels of a nested structure applying operators and part specifications. Query[op1, op2][data] applies op1 at the top level and op2 at the next, which is exactly how Dataset indexing works internally. It also works on plain nested lists and associations, so queries can be written once and reused.
tools.example:
data = {<|"a" -> 1|>, <|"a" -> 2|>};
Query[All, "a"][data]
Query[Select[#a > 1 &], "a"][data]
Query[Total, "a"][data]
Query[GroupBy["a"], Length][data]
tools.notes: Queries are ordinary expressions, so they can be stored in variables and composed; failures give Failure objects rather than errors.

tools.name: Normal
tools.description: Converts an optimized or special-form object into an ordinary expression. It turns a SparseArray into a full list, a Dataset into nested lists and associations, a SeriesData into a plain polynomial, and an InterpolatingFunction or model object into explicit form. An optional second argument restricts which heads are converted.
tools.example:
Normal[SparseArray[{{1, 1} -> 1}, {2, 2}]]
Normal[Series[Exp[x], {x, 0, 4}]]
Normal[Dataset[{<|"a" -> 1|>}]]
Normal[LinearModelFit[data, x, x]]
tools.notes: Normal on a large SparseArray materializes the full dense array and can exhaust memory; check Dimensions first.

tools.name: Missing
tools.description: Represents a value that is absent or could not be determined, carrying a reason such as "KeyAbsent" or "NotAvailable" and optional extra data. It is returned by Lookup and Association access for unknown keys, by Import for empty data cells, and by curated data functions. Missing values propagate through most operations rather than raising errors, so they can be filtered out at the end.
tools.example:
<|"a" -> 1|>["b"]
Missing["NotAvailable"]
MissingQ[Missing["KeyAbsent", "x"]]
Cases[data, Except[_Missing]]
tools.notes: Use MissingQ to test, DeleteMissing to drop, and the Missing handling options of statistical functions to control how they are treated.

tools.name: DeleteMissing
tools.description: Removes Missing entries from a list or Association, optionally descending a given number of levels and requiring a minimum number of present values. It is the standard cleanup step before statistics on imported data. For nested structures, the level and count arguments let you drop whole rows that are too incomplete.
tools.usage:
DeleteMissing[expr]
DeleteMissing[expr, n]
DeleteMissing[expr, n, m]
tools.example:
DeleteMissing[{1, Missing[], 3}]
DeleteMissing[<|"a" -> 1, "b" -> Missing[]|>]
DeleteMissing[{{1, Missing[]}, {2, 3}}, 2]
Mean[DeleteMissing[column]]

tools.name: SparseArray
tools.description: Stores an array by recording only its non-default elements, making very large mostly-empty matrices practical. SparseArray[{pos -> val, ...}, dims] builds one from explicit rules, patterns like {i_, i_} -> 1 fill whole diagonals, and Band specifies diagonals directly. Sparse arrays work with Dot, LinearSolve, Eigenvalues and the other linear algebra functions, which use sparse algorithms automatically.
tools.usage:
SparseArray[{pos1 -> val1, ...}, dims]
SparseArray[{pos -> val}, dims, default]
SparseArray[Band[{i, j}] -> val, dims]
SparseArray[denseArray]

parameters.name: dims
parameters.description: Dimensions of the array; inferred from the positions if omitted.

parameters.name: default
parameters.description: Value of all unspecified elements, 0 by default.

tools.example:
s = SparseArray[{{1, 1} -> 1, {2, 2} -> 2}, {3, 3}];
Normal[s]
SparseArray[{i_, i_} -> 1, {100, 100}]
SparseArray[Band[{1, 2}] -> -1, {5, 5}]
LinearSolve[SparseArray[{{i_, i_} -> 2, {i_, j_} /; Abs[i - j] == 1 -> -1}, {500, 500}], Range[500]] // Short
tools.notes: Use ArrayRules to see the stored rules and Normal to expand to a dense array. Sparse arrays are usually much faster for structured matrices arising from PDE discretizations and graphs.

tools.name: Nothing
tools.description: A symbol that automatically disappears from any list in which it appears, so mapping a function that returns Nothing filters elements out without a separate Select pass. It is the idiomatic way to conditionally omit an item while building a list. Nothing is removed as soon as the enclosing List is evaluated.
tools.notes: Nothing only vanishes inside List, not inside other heads; use Sequence[] for the general case.

tools.name: Dispatch
tools.description: Converts a long list of replacement rules into an optimized dispatch table with hashed lookup, so applying it with /. is near constant time per subexpression instead of linear in the number of rules. Build it once and reuse it whenever thousands of literal rules must be applied repeatedly. The resulting DispatchQ object is used exactly like the original rule list.
tools.notes: Dispatch helps most with many literal (non-pattern) left-hand sides; for pattern rules an Association plus Lookup is often simpler.
